**Program Design & Activities** (~800 words)

The program is grounded in a simple theory of change: when early-elementary students who are reading below grade level receive consistent, individualized literacy instruction during the school year and summer, supported by family engagement that extends reading practice into the home, they will reach grade-level proficiency at higher rates and sustain those gains over time. A one-page logic model is included as Attachment [X] and summarizes the relationship among inputs, activities, outputs, and outcomes described below.

**How the program works**

The program operates on a continuous, year-round cycle with three interconnected components — weekly one-to-one tutoring, family literacy nights, and a six-week summer boost — each designed to address a specific barrier identified in the Statement of Need.

*Weekly one-to-one tutoring* is the program's core instructional activity. Each of the 120 enrolled students is matched with a trained tutor for one 45-minute session per week during the 36-week school year, held in dedicated space at Westside Elementary immediately after dismissal. Sessions follow a structured, evidence-based curriculum aligned with the Science of Reading framework, emphasizing phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension (Scarborough, 2001; National Reading Panel, 2000). Tutors use each student's MAP Growth diagnostic data to set individualized learning targets and adjust instruction on a six-week cycle. The Program Coordinator builds tutor-student matches and schedules, the Lead Literacy Specialist trains and supervises all tutors, and a team of 10 part-time tutors — recruited from local university education programs and required to hold or be pursuing at least a bachelor's degree in education or a related field — delivers the sessions. This model mirrors the dosage and structure used by proven programs such as Reading Partners, which has demonstrated statistically significant gains in fluency and comprehension in randomized controlled trials (MDRC, 2016).

*Family literacy nights* address the home-environment barriers documented in our needs assessment, particularly the finding that only 29% of Westside households report having more than five age-appropriate books at home. These events are held once per month during the school year (nine sessions total) in the Westside Elementary cafeteria, each running 90 minutes on a weekday evening. Every session includes three elements: a 20-minute parent/caregiver workshop on a practical reading strategy (for example, dialogic reading or vocabulary-building during daily routines), 40 minutes of guided parent-child reading practice, and distribution of two free, culturally relevant books for the family to take home. Light dinner and on-site childcare for siblings are provided to remove attendance barriers. The Family Engagement Specialist plans and facilitates these events with support from the Program Coordinator and two volunteers. Research on family literacy programming shows that when caregivers learn specific techniques for shared reading, children's oral language and print awareness improve significantly beyond what tutoring alone achieves (Sénéchal & Young, 2008).

*The six-week summer boost* directly targets the 2.8-month average summer reading loss documented among Westside students. Running Monday through Thursday for six weeks in June and July at Westside Elementary, the program serves all 120 enrolled students in two rotating cohorts of 60. Each day includes 90 minutes of small-group literacy instruction (groups of six, led by tutors) and 60 minutes of enrichment activities — read-alouds, creative writing, library visits — designed to build motivation and reading identity. The Lead Literacy Specialist oversees curriculum and instruction, the Program Coordinator manages logistics and attendance tracking, and the same tutor team delivers instruction, providing continuity of relationships from the school-year component. Meta-analytic evidence indicates that structured summer literacy programs of at least five weeks can eliminate summer loss and produce net gains for low-income elementary students (Kim & Quinn, 2013).

**Participant pathway**

Each student's journey follows four stages. At intake (September), the Program Coordinator reviews MAP Growth scores, confirms eligibility, and conducts a family orientation. During active programming (October through May), the student attends weekly tutoring while the family is invited to monthly literacy nights. At the summer bridge (June through July), the student participates in the six-week boost. At year-end review (August), the team administers a post-assessment, reviews progress, and determines whether the student continues into the next program year or transitions out at grade level. Students who reach proficiency mid-year are celebrated and may shift to a maintenance schedule of biweekly sessions, freeing slots for waitlisted peers.

**Quarterly implementation timeline**

In Quarter 1 (July–September of Year 1), we will finalize the data-sharing agreement with Springfield School District, hire and onboard the Lead Literacy Specialist and tutor team, procure curriculum materials, and conduct student intake and family orientation. In Quarter 2 (October–December), weekly tutoring and monthly family literacy nights will launch at full enrollment of 120 students, with the first six-week progress check completed in November. In Quarter 3 (January–March), programming continues, mid-year MAP Growth assessments are administered and reviewed, and tutor learning plans are adjusted based on results. In Quarter 4 (April–June), school-year tutoring and literacy nights conclude, end-of-year assessments are administered, and the summer boost begins in June. This quarterly cycle repeats in Years 2 and 3, with start-up activities replaced by returning-student re-enrollment and continuous improvement based on evaluation findings from the prior year.

This section presents three measurable objectives that correspond directly to the program's three core activities, followed by an evaluation plan describing how we will collect, analyze, and use data to track progress and improve programming.

**Objectives**

All three objectives use the same measurement structure: a specific target population, a quantified outcome, a defined timeframe, a baseline, and a named assessment instrument. Objectives are set for Year 1; targets for Years 2 and 3 will be adjusted upward based on findings, with proposed benchmarks of 55% and 65% for Objective 1, respectively.

*Objective 1 — Reading proficiency (tutoring).* By the end of Year 1, 45% of enrolled K–3 students (n=54 of 120) will reach at-or-above grade-level reading on the MAP Growth Reading assessment, up from a baseline of 0% of enrolled students at program entry (measured at intake and year-end by district MAP tests).

*Objective 2 — Summer learning retention (summer boost).* By August of Year 1, 70% of students who complete the six-week summer boost (n=84, assuming 100 of 120 complete) will maintain or improve their spring MAP Growth Reading score, compared with a district-documented average summer loss of 2.8 months among Westside peers not enrolled in summer programming (measured by spring and late-summer MAP Growth administrations).

*Objective 3 — Family engagement and home reading practice (family literacy nights).* By the end of Year 1, 60% of participating families (n=72 of 120) will report reading with their child at home at least four times per week, up from a baseline established at program entry through a family reading habits survey (measured at intake and year-end by the same survey instrument).

Together, these three objectives capture the program's intended impact across its core theory of change: direct skill-building through tutoring, loss prevention through summer programming, and home-environment change through family engagement. Outputs — number of tutoring sessions delivered, family literacy nights held, summer boost days completed, and books distributed — will be tracked alongside outcomes but are reported separately in quarterly progress reports.

**Evaluation Plan**

*Design.* The evaluation uses a pre-post design with repeated measures at three points during each program year: intake (September), mid-year (January), and year-end (May/August). Where feasible, we will also employ a quasi-experimental comparison to strengthen causal claims, described below.

*Baseline sources.* Baseline reading proficiency for each student will be drawn from the MAP Growth Reading assessment administered by Springfield School District at the start of the school year, obtained under the existing data-sharing agreement. Baseline family reading habits will be established through a brief intake survey (12 items, available in English and Spanish) administered by the Family Engagement Specialist during family orientation in September. These two sources — one standardized and externally administered, one program-collected — provide both a validated academic measure and a self-reported behavioral measure at entry.

*Data collection tools and frequency.* Reading proficiency will be measured three times per year using MAP Growth, which is already administered district-wide in fall, winter, and spring windows; a fourth administration in late summer will capture summer boost effects and will be coordinated with the school district. Family reading habits will be measured twice per year — at intake and year-end — via the family survey, with a short mid-year pulse check (four items) distributed at the January family literacy night. Tutoring session attendance, dosage, and fidelity will be tracked weekly by tutors in a shared program database. Family literacy night attendance will be recorded at each event by the Family Engagement Specialist.

*Responsibility.* The Program Coordinator holds primary responsibility for data collection, entry, and reporting. The Lead Literacy Specialist reviews MAP Growth results and translates them into instructional adjustments. The Family Engagement Specialist administers and collects family surveys. An external evaluator, contracted on a part-time basis (budgeted in Section 8), will conduct the annual analysis, produce a year-end evaluation report, and present findings to staff and the board.

*Comparison-group approach.* Because all eligible students at Westside Elementary are invited to participate, a randomized control group is not ethical or practical. Instead, the external evaluator will construct a matched comparison group using de-identified MAP Growth data from students in demographically similar elementary schools within Springfield School District who are not receiving comparable programming. Matching criteria will include grade level, baseline MAP score, free/reduced-price lunch status, and English Learner classification. This quasi-experimental approach allows us to estimate program effects above and beyond typical growth, while acknowledging its limitations relative to a randomized design.

*Using findings for improvement.* Data will feed a continuous improvement cycle. After each MAP Growth administration, the Lead Literacy Specialist will convene a tutor review meeting to examine student-level progress, identify students who are not on track, and adjust learning plans. Mid-year family survey results will inform changes to literacy night content and scheduling. The external evaluator's annual report will include actionable recommendations, which the Program Coordinator will incorporate into a written improvement plan shared with the funder in each annual progress report.

*Dashboard metrics.* Staff and leadership will monitor program health through a quarterly dashboard tracking seven indicators: number of students actively enrolled, average tutoring attendance rate, percentage of students on track to meet Objective 1 at year-end, number of family literacy nights held, average family literacy night attendance, percentage of families meeting the four-times-per-week home reading target, and summer boost completion rate. The dashboard will be maintained by the Program Coordinator and reviewed monthly by the Program Director.

**Personnel and fringe.** Salaries for the Program Director, Lead Literacy Specialist, and Program Coordinator are based on the organization's current pay scale and are consistent with Bureau of Labor Statistics median wages for comparable roles in the Springfield metropolitan area. Fringe is calculated at 20% of combined salary costs and covers FICA, workers' compensation, and health insurance contributions. The Program Director provides strategic oversight and funder reporting. The Lead Literacy Specialist trains and supervises tutors, reviews assessment data, and adjusts curriculum. The Program Coordinator manages enrollment, scheduling, data entry, and day-to-day logistics across all three program components.

**Tutors.** Ten part-time tutors are engaged as hourly staff at $20 per hour, each working an average of five hours per week across the 36-week school year. Summer boost instruction is delivered within the same hourly budget by concentrating tutor hours into the six-week session.

**Books and materials.** The $6,000 allocation provides approximately two books per student per month during the school year, distributed at family literacy nights and tutoring sessions, plus consumable instructional materials for the summer boost. Assuming the Year 1 target of 45% reaching grade-level proficiency (n=54), the cost per student reaching proficiency is approximately $3,333. These per-participant figures are competitive with comparable evidence-based tutoring programs nationally, which typically range from $1,500 to $3,000 per student per year (MDRC, *Costs of Implementing High-Impact Tutoring*, 2023).
